title: Housing costs are constraining household formation, mobility, and entry into stable place
source_unit: Harvard Joint Center for Housing Studies, The State of the Nation’s Housing 2026; national housing-market, Census, ACS, and administrative-source synthesis
geography: United States; national and selected metro, income, tenure, age, race, and migration comparisons

young_adult_formation_constraint.value: many young adults are doubling up or living with family rather than forming new households

observations.method: JCHS synthesis of household-growth, labor-market, student-debt, consumer-sentiment, and housing-demand evidence.
observations.uncertainty: The report describes population-level housing and household trends; it does not track the same young adults’ decisions or identify the causal contribution of each financial and labor-market factor.
observations.subgroup: Young adults and U.S. households; the household-growth figures are national totals.
observations.counterinterpretation: Household formation also reflects changing preferences, family support, education, partnership patterns, migration, and local housing supply—not affordability alone.

denominator.unit: percent of U.S. households that relocated in 2024

homeowner_mobility.unit: percent of homeowners moving in 2024; 5.5 percent in 2023

migration_pattern.value: interstate moves and gains in historically fast-growth states slowed; the Midwest recorded net inflows in 2025

observations.method: JCHS analysis of American Community Survey mobility estimates and domestic-migration patterns.
observations.uncertainty: Mobility rates describe whether households moved, not whether they wanted to move, could afford to move, improved their situation, or experienced involuntary displacement.
observations.subgroup: U.S. households by tenure, with regional migration patterns reported separately.
observations.counterinterpretation: Low mobility can reflect satisfaction, aging, remote work, social ties, mortgage-rate lock-in, job conditions, or high transaction costs in addition to housing unaffordability.

median_home_price_to_income.unit: approximately five times median household income in 2025, versus 3.2 in the 1990s

median_home_payment.unit: U.S. dollars monthly for a median-priced home under stated financing assumptions in 2025

under_35_homeownership.unit: share of households under age 35 owning a home

affordable_listings_under_75000_income.value: 23 percent in March 2026; 49 percent in March 2019
affordable_listings_under_75000_income.unit: listings affordable to a household earning $75,000 or less

observations.method: JCHS synthesis of national home prices, mortgage-payment calculations, homeownership rates, and listing affordability estimates.
observations.uncertainty: Payment affordability depends on down payment, interest rate, taxes, insurance, debt, household income, and metro location; listing affordability is not the same as successful purchase or access to credit.
observations.subgroup: Would-be buyers, especially younger adults and households with moderate incomes; racial homeownership gaps are also reported in the source.
observations.counterinterpretation: Home equity, household transfers, local prices, shared ownership, and non-market housing can buffer some households even as national entry conditions worsen.

observations.period: 2019–2024; homeowner cost burden and insurance/energy exposure

homeowner_cost_burden.unit: percent spending more than 30 percent of income on housing in 2024

severely_burdened_homeowners.unit: million households spending more than half of income on housing

monthly_insurance_premium_change.unit: percent increase from 2019 to 2025, reaching $201 average monthly premium

low_income_homeowner_burden.unit: percent of homeowners earning under $30,000 who were cost burdened in 2024

observations.method: JCHS tabulations of ACS and cited mortgage, property-tax, energy, and insurance sources.
observations.uncertainty: Cost burden is a spending threshold, not a direct measure of housing quality, arrears, foreclosure, insurance adequacy, or health; sources are not a same-household longitudinal panel.
observations.subgroup: Homeowners overall and by income, age, race, and hazard-exposed market where reported.
observations.counterinterpretation: Home equity and fixed-rate debt can improve net wealth for some owners while non-mortgage costs create immediate budget pressure; national averages conceal large local differences.

renter_cost_burden.unit: percent spending more than 30 percent of income on housing in 2024

severely_burdened_renters.unit: million renter households spending more than half of income on housing

cost_burden_change_since_2019.unit: million additional cost-burdened renter households since 2019

low_rent_units_under_1000.value: down more than 30 percent, or more than 7 million units, from 2014 to 2024 in inflation-adjusted terms

extremely_low_income_supply.unit: affordable and available rental units per 100 extremely low-income households in 2024

rental_assistance_reach.unit: approximately one in four very low-income renter households receiving a housing subsidy

observations.method: JCHS tabulations of ACS, NLIHC, rental-market, and federal housing-assistance data.
observations.uncertainty: Cost burden and unit counts do not measure eviction, homelessness, skipped meals, delayed care, or whether a household receives informal support; affordability definitions vary by income and location.
observations.subgroup: Renter households, with emphasis on low- and extremely-low-income renters and historically disadvantaged racial groups.
observations.counterinterpretation: New supply, shared housing, vouchers, local protections, and household income changes can improve conditions for particular renters even while the national low-cost stock shrinks.

related_sources.claim: Direct PDF of the 2026 report and its figures, tables, and methods notes.
JCHS release summarizing the report’s affordability, household-growth, and mobility findings.

boundary: This record identifies a national U.S. housing trend in which affordability pressure is constraining household formation, mobility, homeownership entry, and renter security. It does not establish a same-household causal pathway, individual housing histories, eviction or homelessness incidence, or that housing costs alone explain changing family structure or migration.
